questions.stem: Which of the following statements represents a valid use of the universal quantifier (∀)?

choices.B: There exists a cat that does not like fish.
choices.C: For every integer x, x + 2 > x.
choices.D: Some numbers are not divisible by themselves.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'For every integer x, x + 2 > x.' This states that the property holds true for all integers. Choice A is false because dogs cannot fly in reality. Choice B uses the existential quantifier (∃), not the universal one. Choice D involves a negation and thus implies the existential quantifier.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) asserts that a property holds for all members of a set or domain. In this case, choice C correctly applies the universal quantifier to the statement about integers.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Confusing the universal quantifier (∀) with the existential quantifier (∃). The latter is used when stating that there exists at least one element in a set satisfying a property.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) correctly to describe all real numbers?

choices.A: There exists a number x such that x^2 = 0.
choices.B: For every x, there is y with y > x.
choices.C: All real numbers have an even integer multiple.
choices.D: No real number is both rational and irrational.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'No real number is both rational and irrational.' This asserts that no member of the set of real numbers can be both rational and irrational at the same time. Choice A uses the existential quantifier, choice B does not involve a negation, and choice C is false since there are real numbers without an even integer multiple.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) describes properties that hold for all elements in a set. In this case, choice D correctly applies the universal quantifier to exclude a specific property from holding for any real number.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that the negation of 'some numbers are both rational and irrational' is a valid use of the universal quantifier.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) to express that all circles have a specific property?

choices.A: There exists a circle with no center.
choices.B: For every circle, there is a line tangent to it.
choices.C: All circles have a circumference-to-diameter ratio of π.
choices.D: Some circles are not perfectly round.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'All circles have a circumference-to-diameter ratio of π.' This property holds true for every circle. Choice A and D use existential quantifiers, and choice B does not express a negation or a specific property shared by all circles.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) can be used to describe properties that are universally true for a class of objects, like circles in this case. Choice C correctly applies the universal quantifier to the circumference-to-diameter ratio.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that the property 'circumference- to-diameter ratio is π' applies to all circles.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) to express a true fact about integers?

choices.B: For every integer x, there exists an integer y such that x + y = 0.
choices.C: No integer is both positive and negative.
choices.D: Some integers have more than two factors.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'For every integer x, there exists an integer y such that x + y = 0.' This is true because for any integer x, its negative (-x) will add up to zero. Choice A is false (2 is even and prime), choice C does not use a quantifier, and choice D uses the existential quantifier.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) can be used to express properties that hold for all elements in a set. In this case, choice B correctly applies the universal quantifier to state that every integer has an additive inverse.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that the property 'every integer has an additive inverse' is true for all integers.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) to express a fact about real numbers?

choices.B: For every real number x, there exists a real number y such that xy = 1.
choices.C: No real number is both positive and negative at the same time.
choices.D: Some real numbers have decimal expansions that terminate.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'No real number is both positive and negative at the same time.' This is true for all real numbers. Choice A is false, choice B uses the existential quantifier, and choice D does not express a negation or a specific property shared by all real numbers.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) can be used to describe properties that are universally true for a class of objects, like real numbers in this case. Choice C correctly applies the universal quantifier to exclude a specific property from holding for any real number.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that no real number can simultaneously be both positive and negative.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) to express a true fact about triangles?

choices.A: All triangles have at least four sides.
choices.B: For every triangle, there exists a circle that can be inscribed within it.
choices.C: No triangle has all three angles equal to 90 degrees.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'For every triangle, there exists a circle that can be inscribed within it.' This property holds true for all triangles. Choice A is false, choice C does not use a quantifier, and choice D uses the existential quantifier.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) can be used to describe properties that are universally true for a class of objects, like triangles in this case. Choice B correctly applies the universal quantifier to state that every triangle has an inscribed circle.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that every triangle has an inscribed circle.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements uses the universal quantifier (∀) to express a true fact about even numbers?

choices.B: For every even number x, there exists an odd number y such that x + y = 0.
choices.C: No even number is both positive and negative.
choices.D: Some even numbers have more than two factors.

questions.solution: The correct statement using the universal quantifier (∀) is 'For every even number x, there exists an odd number y such that x + y = 0.' This is true because for any even number x, its negative (-x) will add up to zero. Choice A is false (2 is even and prime), choice C does not use a quantifier, and choice D uses the existential quantifier.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier (∀) can be used to express properties that hold for all elements in a set. In this case, choice B correctly applies the universal quantifier to state that every even number has an odd additive inverse.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Not recognizing that the property 'every even number has an odd additive inverse' is true for all even numbers.
